newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh central bank chief woos foreign banks.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh central bank chief woos foreign banks.

text.p: Bangladesh's new central bank Governor Lutfar Rahman Sarkar said on Monday the country needed foreign resources and technology to spur investment.

"We believe that increased participation by the foreign banks will set up forces for improvement in efficiency through skill formation and technology uptake," Sarkar, who took over as the central bank chief on Thursday, told a reception marking the opening of South Korean Hanil Bank.
Hanil Bank officials said on Monday its bank branch, set up in September, would mainly finance projects by Korean investors.
The government had removed most of the stumbling blocks that stood in the way of easy movement of foreign capital through the banking channel, Sarkar said.

Bangladesh has already passed a law in Parliament allowing a separate exclusive investment zone in the country by South Korean investors, and Hanil bank officials said about 130 industrial units were expected to be set up in the zone.
"We see more than $1.0 billion in Korean investment coming in to Bangladesh in the next 10 years," one official said.

Further attractions for foreign investors include cheap labour. "Cheap labour of Bangladesh is the chief attraction for them (foreign investors)," Sarkar said. "I guess, in two-decades' time from now, Bangladesh will have booming export processing activities...the demand for financial services will grow enormously."
Sarkar said the number of foreign bank operating in Bangladesh has already risen to 10 from six in 1990.
He said Bangladesh had been praised for its "notable macroeconomic stability" through fundamental reforms in economy.

But "the results have been mixed. Our external position has improved significantly. Inflation is under control, investment is picking up gradually, but the much awaited economic growth is still short of our expectation," he said.

Sarkar said gross domestic product (GDP) has grown an average 4.5 percent for more than a decade. But "what we need is a boost in investment from about 14 percent of GDP to around 20 percent to achieve a respectable growth performances."
